title: Between standing and lying
hook: the night before the council, Ananda gives up striving, lies down, and is freed before his head reaches the pillow (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
carry: before his head reached the pillow

segments.voice: Yesterday, the teacher had died, and Ananda wept, still unawakened. Your line was soon, not now. Were you patient with yourself somewhere, even once? Tonight the council is one day away, and Ananda is still not there. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

A deadline, and a sacred one. The elders are gathering at Rajagaha to recite the teaching together, and in the Vinaya's account every one of them has already reached the end of the path. Every one except Ananda. He's the man who walked beside the Buddha, carried his water, heard the discourses day after day. And he hasn't arrived. So on the last night he does the obvious thing with a deadline. He works. He practices hard, attending to the body, hour after hour, pushing at a door that won't open. Then, toward dawn, he stops pushing. He decides to lie down. Today is about what happens in that small space, between standing and lying.
screen: `A COUNCIL TOMORROW.` → `EVERYONE ARRIVED BUT ONE.` → `HE PUSHES ALL NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the push. The Vinaya says Ananda spent much of that night in mindfulness of the body. This isn't a lazy man looking for a shortcut. It's a careful one, doing the practice the way he was taught. And still, by effort alone, nothing gives. Second, the letting go. Toward dawn he thinks: let me lie down. He isn't quitting the path. He's setting down the strain. A later commentary adds a reason. It says he saw that his effort had grown too tight, and he eased it. Third, the moment itself. He leans his body toward the bed. And the text says that before his head reached the pillow, and while his feet had not yet left the ground, his mind was freed. Not sitting. Not walking. Not lying down. Somewhere in between. It's a detail worth staying with: the thing he had chased for so long came in a moment that doesn't even have a name. Fourth, what it says to an ordinary evening. Ananda didn't stop practicing. He had practiced for a long time, and that practice was the ground under his feet. What he stopped was the clutching. The story doesn't say effort is useless. It says effort can tighten into a fist, and a closed fist can't receive anything. In the morning, the account goes on, he took his place among the elders as one of them.
screen: `HE PUSHED ALL NIGHT.` · `HE LET GO, AND LAY DOWN.` · `BEFORE HIS HEAD TOUCHED THE PILLOW.` · `EFFORT, WITHOUT THE FIST.` · then, large: `BETWEEN STANDING AND LYING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop straining, for once. Settle where you are, and notice where you're pushing right now. The jaw. The shoulders. The space between the eyebrows. Maybe even the breath, being managed. Let one of those go, the way Ananda let himself lie down. You're not giving anything up. You're only setting down the extra. If you catch yourself working hard at relaxing, notice that too, and smile at it. Then stay with the breath as it is, without trying to improve it. The bell holds the time.
Arahant. What Ananda becomes the night before the council, freed between standing and lying, before his head reaches the pillow. Today's word.

Your line: before his head reached the pillow. Today, when you catch yourself straining at something that won't move, put it down for one breath, and see what comes into the gap. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Teachers in several Buddhist traditions tell Ananda's last night as a story about balanced effort, and recall it for students whose practice has grown tight and forced.

myth: that night Ananda gave up the path
he set down the strain, not the practice; in the morning he joined the elders as one of them.
he was freed while sitting in meditation
it came as he leaned down to rest, before his head reached the pillow.

fork.setup: you're Ananda. it's nearly dawn, the council is tomorrow, and pushing hasn't worked. what do you do?
options: set down the strain and lie down.
fork.reveal: he decides to lie down, and before his head reaches the pillow his mind is freed. the release comes when the clutching stops.

original.note: Pali arahant: one who has reached the end of the path, as the elders of the council had.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about giving up.
what it means: Ananda set down the strain, not the path, and was freed in the gap between postures.
what a scholar hears: the Vinaya's account of the first council (Cullavagga 11) tells it; later commentaries add that he saw his effort had grown too tight.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Cullavagga 11 (the first council; Ananda's awakening the night before)
Sumangalavilasini (Digha Nikaya commentary), introduction: account of the first council

notes: All paraphrased; Rhys Davids and Oldenberg translated the Cullavagga (SBE 20) but the writer was not certain of the exact wording, so nothing is quoted.
Confirm that Cullavagga 11 says the other elders were all arahants and Ananda alone was not, and that he spent much of the night in mindfulness of the body (kayagatasati).
'Before his head reached the pillow and while his feet had not left the ground' paraphrases the Vinaya; confirm wording.
The reason (his effort had grown too tight, and he eased it) is attributed to 'a later commentary'; confirm it is in the Sumangalavilasini's council account (or name the right commentary).
'Some teachers like this detail best' is deliberately soft; the 'in none of the four postures' framing is commentarial.
'In the morning he took his place among the elders': commentaries embellish his arrival (e.g. appearing through the earth); kept plain.
Original: अरहन्त (arahant); confirm Devanagari form and pronunciation guide.

Editor: softened 'of the holiest kind' and 'some teachers like this detail best of all' (unsourced superlatives); replaced the myth item 'Ananda was already awakened' because day 736 used nearly the same item.
Auditor: the Vinaya times the moment 'toward dawn' (rattiya paccusasamayam), not 'late in the night'; corrected in the hook, teach, match pair and fork.
